To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the complexity of all optical-computing implementations is exponential in the number of input bits, and that the complexity of a particular implementation can be reduced to within a constant factor of the best possible realization of a Boolean-function.

(1) the complexity of optical-computational systems is exponential in the number of inputs and (2) the best optical realization of a function is no more complex than the best theoretical implementation.

the complexity of any optical-computing system, as measured by any of several metrics (time, space-bandwidth, area), is exponential in the number of inputs, except for one system that is optimal to within a constant factor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the complexity of optical computing systems, and the results are relevant to all optical-computing implementations.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
optical-computing implementations of logic functions require an exponential increase in the system complexity as a function of the number of inputs.
optical computing, at this stage, is a viable approach for the realization of small to moderate size Boolean functions.
optical computing has not, as of yet, demonstrated a significant advantage over conventional electronic computing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the optical-computing approach is promising, it has yet to be demonstrated that the complexity of optical computing can be reduced to a polynomial function of the size of the problem.
optical computing is not inherently parallel and is no more powerful than digital computers.
optical computing is not a panacea for the solution of all computational problems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the exponential growth in the complexity of optical-computations is not an intrinsic property of optics, but is rather a property of the implementations proposed so far.

the complexity of any optical-computing paradigm that is to be used for general purpose computing must grow at least as fast as the complexity of the best possible implementation of a Boolean function in that paradigm.

, in order to achieve the full potential of optical-computational architectures, one must use the full power of the optical system, including the ability to perform operations on an arbitrary set of inputs.
